metadata.methods_description: Participants sat in a sound-isolating booth and heard stimuli through ER-2 insert earphones at about 60 dB SPL. Phase one presented ten one-minute click trials. Phase two presented 33 shuffled trials each of original and chimeric monophonic music, with 0.5 s pauses between trials. EEG was recorded in BrainVision format. Stimuli were controlled with a Python script using expyfun. Participants also completed a musicianship questionnaire.

citation_details.title: Hierarchical Neural Representations and Divergence Mechanisms in Music and Speech Processing
citation_details.author: Amelia Duarte, Amelia Lindholm, Julian Thorne
citation_details.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH & SOCIAL SCIENCES
citation_details.abstract: The human auditory system possesses an extraordinary capacity to parse complex acoustic environments, extracting meaningful communicative and affective signals from overlapping sensory streams. Among the most intricate of these signals are music and speech, two distinctly human faculties that share fundamental acoustic properties such as pitch, rhythm, and timbre, yet serve divergent communicative and emotional functions. This paper investigates the hierarchical neural representations and divergence mechanisms underlying the processing of music and speech. By synthesizing current perspectives in cognitive neuroscience, auditory processing, and neuroimaging, we elucidate how the brain utilizes shared neural substrates at the peripheral and early cortical stages before deploying specialized, divergent pathways in higher-order association areas.
